title: Ultrasonic Weld Inspection | Angle-Beam UT, US Sites
description: Ultrasonic weld inspection in the US: angle-beam UT to AWS D1.1, D1.5, ASME Section V and B31.3, with rated indications and a clear report. Request a quote.
h1: Ultrasonic Weld Inspection: Angle-Beam UT of Groove Welds Across the United States
html:
Ultrasonic weld inspection uses a manual angle-beam (shear wave) probe to find planar flaws such as lack of fusion, incomplete penetration and cracks inside groove welds in steel. Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to fabrication shops, erection sites and plants across the United States, scans welds to your code and procedure, and reports every recorded indication with its location, rating and accept or reject call. To scope the work, request a UT inspection quote with the weld map and governing code.

What ultrasonic weld testing finds

A shear wave probe sends sound into the weld at a fixed refracted angle, commonly 45, 60 or 70 degrees in steel. A flaw that reflects the beam back to the probe appears as a signal on the screen at a position that tells the technician how far along the beam the reflector is and, from that, its depth and location along the weld. The method is strongest on flat, planar flaws that face the sound path: lack of sidewall fusion, lack of root fusion, incomplete joint penetration, and cracks. It is also reasonably good at slag lines and porosity clusters, although those rounded flaws reflect less sound than a planar one of similar size.

It is not a pass or fail by feel. The acceptance rules in the code define a reference level, a method of rating each indication against that level, and length and rating limits by weld thickness and loading. The technician records what the code requires, and the owner or the code decides what is rejectable.

Codes that govern UT of welds

The code that applies to the weld decides the technique, the reference level, the scanning pattern and the acceptance limits. These are the ones we are asked about most in the United States.

  • AWS D1.1: structural welding code for steel, with ultrasonic examination of groove welds in Clause 8 Part F, used in buildings, plant structures and steel fabrication.
  • AWS D1.5: bridge welding code, used for highway and rail bridge girders and with its own acceptance tables for tension and compression members.
  • ASME Section V, Article 4: the ultrasonic examination methods for welds that other ASME code sections reference.
  • ASME B31.3: process piping, which requires ultrasonic examination to the manner stated in paragraph 344.6 when UT is used in place of radiography or is specified by the owner.
  • API 1104: pipeline girth welds, where the standard allows ultrasonic examination as a method alongside radiography under its qualification requirements.

The weld inspection overview is on the weld inspection page, and the requirements of Article 4 are explained in this guide to ASME Section V Article 4.

Technique: reference level, coverage and scanning

A weld UT job starts with the base material. A straight-beam scan of the strip beside the weld confirms there are no laminations that would block or distort the angle beam; AWS D1.1 and the procedure may require this before the weld is scanned. The surface is cleaned of spatter and weld ripples so the probe couples, and the weld is marked with datum lines and stationing.

The technician calibrates the horizontal sweep on a calibration block such as the IIW block, sets the beam angle and probe index point, and builds a reference level from a known reflector. In the AWS system, a signal from the reference reflector is set to a standard height and every indication is then rated in decibels against that reference, with a correction for sound lost along the path. ASME procedures use a distance-amplitude correction curve built from side-drilled holes in a basic calibration block of similar material. Each system has its own details, and the written procedure follows the code on the drawing.

Scanning follows a pattern, not a walk along the weld. The probe moves toward and away from the weld to cover the full volume, with lateral movement along it and a small swing or oscillation to catch differently oriented flaws. Multiple angles may be needed so the beam meets both fusion faces. The technician scans from both sides of the weld where access allows, because a flaw reflects better from the face it points toward. A weld that can only be scanned from one side, a weld with an uneven cap, or a weld in thick material with a root that cannot be reached from the flat surface may need a modified technique or an agreed limitation, and that belongs in the report.

Where UT in place of radiography has limits

Buyers sometimes ask us to replace radiography with ultrasonic testing on pressure vessel welds, and the answer depends on the code. ASME Section VIII Division 1 permits ultrasonic examination in place of radiography only under conditions set out in Code Case 2235 and Appendix 12, and those conditions call for computerized imaging techniques, with recorded data, that Atlantis does not offer on this page. Manual angle-beam UT of the kind described here is accepted for the examinations where the code lists it directly: structural welds under AWS D1.1 and D1.5, welds in B31.3 piping where the owner specifies UT, and many shop and repair applications under a procedure the owner approves.

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States, because industrial radiography is licensed under 10 CFR Part 34 and Agreement State rules. If your drawing demands radiographic examination or a computerized ultrasonic technique, tell us up front and we will say plainly whether this work fits. If the scope is a repair or a fit-up check where a code-permitted ultrasonic method applies, we can scan it.

Weld joints and materials we scan

Typical weld UT jobs
Joint or productAccess and techniqueTypical code
Beam and column groove weldsSingle or double sided, 45 to 70 degree shear waveAWS D1.1
Bridge girder flange and web splicesBoth-side scan, indications rated by stress categoryAWS D1.5
Pressure vessel and heat exchanger shell weldsContact scan from the outside surface, reference level from the procedureASME Section V Article 4
Process piping butt weldsContact scan on the pipe surface after cap preparationASME B31.3
Pipeline girth weldsSurface-prepared scan where the owner qualifies UTAPI 1104
Plate and nozzle welds, build-up and repairsAngle-beam coverage with straight-beam base scanContract specification

Carbon steel and low-alloy steel are the standard case. Austenitic stainless and nickel alloys scatter and bend sound because of their grain structure, so ultrasonic weld testing on those welds needs special probes and a qualification block of the same material. We tell you at the quote stage if the material takes the job outside the method.

What the weld UT report contains

  • Weld identification, weld map or joint number, material, thickness and diameter or length
  • Procedure number and revision, code edition, acceptance criteria and the beam angles used
  • Equipment, probe frequency and angle, calibration block and calibration checks
  • Technician name and ultrasonic level, with the written practice the qualification sits under
  • Each recorded indication with station, depth, length, amplitude or rating and the rejection decision against the stated criteria
  • A sketch or marked weld map, areas not scanned, and any limitation on coverage

A Level II technician performs and interprets the scan; an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews the report. For help writing a weld UT procedure, see NDT technical procedure development and procedure qualification and demonstration.

What to send for a quote

  • Governing code and edition, acceptance table and any owner supplements
  • Weld map or joint list with material, thickness, joint type and quantity
  • Drawings showing access, backing, and whether both sides can be scanned
  • Surface condition, welding process and whether welds are as-welded or ground flush
  • Whether a written procedure exists or has to be provided, and who approves it
  • Site address, badging and safety requirements, and the schedule driver, such as an erection sequence or turnaround window

Where we work in the United States

Weld UT work is concentrated where heavy fabrication, steel and energy construction are. These city pages carry local context:

  • Houston: module and vessel fabrication yards and plant construction along the Gulf Coast.
  • Pittsburgh: steel structure, bridge and mill-fabricated products in the Ohio Valley.
  • Chicago: structural steel, rail and heavy equipment shops across the Chicago area.
  • Tulsa: pressure vessel, tank and pipeline fabrication in the midcontinent.
  • Cleveland: steel mills, machinery and fabrication shops in northern Ohio.
  • Birmingham: steel, pipe and foundry products in the Southeast.
  • Milwaukee: heavy equipment and mining machinery welding.
  • Norfolk: shipyard and marine structure welding on the Hampton Roads waterfront.

See how the work reads in each sector: fabrication shops, steel mills and structural steel, offshore platforms, marine and shipyards, wind towers and pipelines. The method overview is on the national ultrasonic testing page.

Planning notes for weld inspection

Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, so the work fits your fabrication schedule rather than ours. Weld UT normally follows visual examination and, where the code calls for it, any hold time after welding; it also needs the weld cooled enough for couplant to stay in place. Access is set by the site: scaffolding, ladders, lifts or rope access, and permits for confined space or work at height. Fit-up and cleanup of the scanning surface go faster when the fabricator grinds the weld ripples and marks the datum before we arrive.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiographic testing in the United States. We do not offer the computerized ultrasonic techniques needed for UT in place of radiography under ASME Section VIII, and we do not name or sell specialist scanning methods on this page. We do not size flaw height for fitness for service decisions, and we do not make the weld acceptance decision when the code gives that to the owner or its inspector.

Training your own UT technicians

If your shop wants its own UT staff, our UT Level 2 training covers angle-beam setup, calibration, scanning and indication evaluation, and the ultrasonic testing simulator lets trainees practice flaw location before they scan a real weld. Manufacturing teams can see manufacturing NDT training. Under SNT-TC-1A the employer certifies its personnel, so the training supports your written practice.

faq.q: What is the difference between ultrasonic weld inspection and shear wave UT?
faq.a: Shear wave UT, also called angle-beam ultrasonic testing, is the technique used for most ultrasonic weld inspection. The probe sends sound into the weld at an angle so it meets planar flaws; the two phrases describe the same work in everyday use.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing replace radiography on a weld?
faq.a: Only where the governing code allows it. Manual angle-beam UT is accepted directly in AWS D1.1, AWS D1.5 and some B31.3 applications. ASME Section VIII UT in place of radiography has conditions that need computerized techniques we do not offer, and we do not perform radiography in the United States.

faq.q: What thickness range can angle-beam UT inspect?
faq.a: Manual angle-beam methods are used on a wide range of steel thicknesses, with the practical lower limit set by probe size and sound path and the upper limit by access and attenuation. The procedure states the range covered, and we confirm it against your weld map before quoting.

faq.q: Do you need access to both sides of the weld?
faq.a: Scanning from both sides gives better coverage because a flaw reflects best toward the face it points at. If only one side is accessible, the procedure may need a modified technique, and the report records the limitation so the owner knows what was covered.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication is rejectable?
faq.a: The acceptance criteria in the governing code or contract decide, and the report states them. Our technician rates the indication against the reference level, and the owner or its inspector makes the final call if the code assigns it to them.

faq.q: What code editions do you work to?
faq.a: We work to the edition named in the contract and procedure, whether it is AWS D1.1, AWS D1.5, ASME Section V Article 4, B31.3 or API 1104. Send the edition and any owner supplements when you request a quote so the written procedure matches.

faq.q: Can you inspect stainless steel and nickel alloy welds?
faq.a: Austenitic and nickel alloy welds scatter and distort sound, so the method needs special probes and qualification blocks of the same material. We review the weld and material before quoting and tell you if the job needs something outside the method.

faq.q: Do you provide a written procedure?
faq.a: Yes, an ASNT Level III can write or review the UT procedure to the governing code, and it is approved before work starts. If your site already has an approved procedure, send it and we follow it.

faq.q: What should be ready on site before the technician arrives?
faq.a: Welds should be visually accepted, cleaned of spatter and ripples where the procedure requires it, marked with a datum and weld number, and accessible with safe access arranged. The better the surface, the more reliable the scan.
